messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ahmed, a 22‑year‑old auditor of Lebanese descent, worked in a bustling downtown office. When he was nineteen, a senior colleague who had been invited to a client dinner took advantage of the crowded, dimly lit room to force himself upon Ahmed. The moment is still fresh in his mind: the metallic tang of the air conditioning, the lingering perfume of the room’s freshly scented candles, and the sudden, sharp movement of the man’s arm as he pushed past Ahmed’s shoulder. The violation was not only physical but moral; Ahmed had been the one who had opened the door for the man and had trusted him as a colleague and a friend. Those sensations—especially the smell of the candles, the man's abrupt movement, and the sense that someone was misbehaving—have become the very triggers that keep him trapped in the aftermath. After the assault, Ahmed began to notice that certain odors—any scent he associated with a locker room or a conference room—would snap him into a state of hypervigilance. The smell itself, or the mere thought of a similar odor, would lead him to rush to the nearest exit, to avoid situations where others might evaluate his performance or appearance, and to dress in concealing clothing that could hide any signs of bruising or stress. He also avoided unfamiliar places, preferring the familiarity of his own office and the routine of audit rooms he had spent years inspecting. The threat of sudden movements and the possibility that any stranger might turn a benign interaction into an assault kept his body constantly tense, a physical reminder that danger lurked behind every door. These reactions are exactly the maladaptive strategies that stem directly from the triggers: when the smell of a candle rises, Ahmed’s first instinct is to stay near an exit, to wear layered clothing, and to keep his eyes peeled for any odd movement. The very act of avoiding the triggers also fed into his negative self‑appraisals. Ahmed began to compare himself to others, thinking that someone more careful or more powerful would not have allowed such an event to happen. He could not shake the feeling that he had somehow failed to keep himself safe. The realization that the people he had trusted—his former friends, the clients he had served—could no longer be trusted eroded his sense of joy. The humiliation of being violated in a place where he had been praised for his diligence left him feeling permanently degraded. The weight of those thoughts—lost happiness, humiliation, and self‑comparison—reinforced his belief that he was the only one who could not protect himself. Maladaptive strategies also amplified Ahmed’s negative appraisals. By constantly staying near exits and concealing himself, he inadvertently made himself the very person that others would look at and judge; the act of hiding his clothes in a line of bright, casual attire caused him to feel more scrutinized and, in turn, more humiliated. The strategies he employed, meant to protect him, only magnified the feeling that he was different and less capable than his peers. Moreover, the very act of keeping his body in a constant state of readiness heightened his sensitivity to normal office noises and movements, turning ordinary greetings into potential threats. In this way, the strategies he used to cope also became new triggers, turning everyday office chatter into a reminder of the assault and reinforcing his sense of danger. The constant alertness and avoidance, in turn, perpetuated the feeling of threat, creating a cycle that tightened around him day after day. In the weeks that followed, the cycle became more pronounced. At the audit firm, Ahmed avoided taking on new client sites, refusing to go to unfamiliar conference rooms or client meetings. When a junior colleague asked him to review a financial report, he would insist on doing it in the back office, close to the elevator, rather than in the bright conference space. His avoidance of unfamiliar places at work, triggered by the fear that someone could harm him, meant he was no longer meeting deadlines and lost opportunities for promotion. The very environment that once gave him pride now reinforced his sense of inadequacy. His body’s constant tension, triggered by the slightest movement or scent, made every audit session feel like a battle rather than a professional task. Each time he stayed near an exit or covered his clothing, he felt the weight of humiliation grow heavier, his belief that he was “broken” hardening. Now, five years after the assault, Ahmed sits on the threshold of a new job interview, heart hammering, body tense. He has avoided the front desk and the receptionist’s smile, fearful that any evaluation might trigger a memory of the violation. It is this fear of being scrutinized—an echo of the humiliation he feels—that has driven him to seek therapy. He tells his therapist that the most terrifying thought is that he will once again feel like a victim, that the world will view him as weak. Yet he also hopes that by confronting these triggers and the maladaptive strategies that bind him, he can reclaim the sense of joy he lost and rebuild his professional identity.
